lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: Dig Here?
case.hook: After we solved the square lakes, a volunteer named Marco wrote me a letter with a big idea. He wants to dig our own phosphate to make fertilizer (plant food) for the Field Station garden. Before anyone grabs a shovel, let’s check his four pins against a real resource map.

body: Phosphate makes fertilizer, right? So let’s dig our own! I put four pins on my map.
Phosphate is probably everywhere in Florida, so any pin should work. Which one should we dig first?

pins.name: Near my cousin’s house in Miami

case.question: Which of Marco’s pins could have phosphate, and why is phosphate found only in some places?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.
case.stillsCredit: Map: Florida shapes from U.S. Census Bureau boundary files (public domain, via us-atlas). Springs: Florida’s first-magnitude springs. Phosphate mines: Bone Valley and Hamilton County mining areas (U.S. Geological Survey). Citrus: the leading citrus counties (USDA). Beaches: Florida’s sandy coast. Symbols are placed by hand and are approximate.

clues.t: Phosphate isn’t everywhere. On the real map, the mines sit in just two small areas: central Florida east of Tampa, and one spot in north Florida.
The map key tells what each symbol means. Phosphate mines are clustered. Beaches follow the coast, and citrus makes a band across the middle.
Phosphate rock formed only where shallow seas once covered parts of Florida. Mines go where the rock is, so the clusters on the map are evidence of what’s underground.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: test the pins
clues.t: Pins 3 (Mulberry) and 4 (White Springs) are inside phosphate clusters. Pins 1 (Miami) and 2 (Pensacola) have no phosphate anywhere near.

solve.title: Where could Marco find phosphate?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Anywhere. Phosphate is spread all over Florida, so every pin works.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Are phosphate mines spread all over the map?

options.t: Only at pins 3 and 4, near Mulberry and White Springs. Phosphate rock formed only where ancient seas left it, and the clusters on the map are the evidence.
options.why: Case cracked! Phosphate is found only in certain places, and the map pattern shows where. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: Only at pins 1 and 2, because Miami and Pensacola are big, busy places.
options.why: Check Clue 4. Does the map show phosphate near Miami or Pensacola?

guessmap.title: Guess first
todo: Pick a resource, then tap the map where you think it is found most.
Press “Show me the real map” and see how close you were.

why.t: Scientists write down what they expect before they look at data. Then they can tell what surprised them.

guessmap.q: Look at the real map. Which resource is found in the fewest places?

opts.t: Beaches
opts.miss: Beaches go all the way around the coast. Which symbol shows up in only a couple of small spots?

opts.t: Phosphate mines
Springs
opts.miss: There are lots of spring dots across north-central Florida. Which symbol shows up in only a couple of small spots?

guessmap.win: Phosphate is found in just two small areas of Florida. Marco thought it was everywhere. That’s a clue.

maplayers.afterText: tell you something about why it's there
maplayers.title: Map layers
todo: Turn on one layer at a time in the map key.
For each layer, pick the pattern you see.
Read all four, then answer the question.

why.t: One set of symbols for one thing. Turning layers on one at a time keeps a busy map easy to read.

patterns.t: Clustered in one or two areas

note.citrus: Groves stretch in a band across central and south-central Florida.
note.beaches: Beaches follow the coast all the way around the state.
note.phosphate: Two small clusters: a big one east of Tampa and a small one in north Florida.
note.springs: Springs cluster in north-central Florida, with a few in the Panhandle.

miss.citrus: Look at the orange shading. Is it in one spot, or does it stretch across the state?
miss.beaches: Where are the beach symbols? Follow the edge of the state.
miss.phosphate: How many places have diamond symbols? Are they spread out or bunched up?
miss.springs: Are the blue dots all over the state, or mostly in one part?

maplayers.q: Marco says phosphate is probably everywhere. What does the phosphate layer show?

opts.t: It’s spread across the whole state.
opts.miss: Turn the phosphate layer on again. Where are the diamonds?

opts.t: It’s clustered in just two small areas.
It’s along the coast, like the beaches.
opts.miss: Look again. Are the diamonds on the coast?

maplayers.win: You read every layer with the map key. Phosphate is clustered, not everywhere. That’s a clue.

whyhere.title: Why here?
todo: Drag the reason that explains the pattern onto it, or tap the reason and then the map.
One reason is a trick. Then answer the question.

causes.t: Water-filled limestone close to the surface

causes.miss: Trick card! Lots of people live in Miami and Jacksonville. Do these symbols follow the big cities?

items.why: Millions of years ago, shallow seas covered these parts of Florida. Phosphate formed in the sea-floor mud and in old bones and teeth.
items.miss: Phosphate is a rock. What made the rock form only in these spots?

items.why: Here the limestone that holds Florida’s underground water is close to the surface, so water pushes up through openings.
items.miss: Springs are water coming out of the ground. Where is that water stored?

items.why: A hard freeze can kill orange trees. Freezes are rarer here than in north Florida.
items.miss: Orange trees can die in a freeze. What kind of weather do they need?

items.why: Waves pile up sand along the shore, so beaches only form on the coast.
items.miss: Where do waves pile up sand?

whyhere.q: So why are phosphate mines found in only a few places?

opts.t: The rock formed only in those places, so the mines go where the rock is.
Miners like to live near the beach.
opts.miss: Look at the phosphate map. Are the mines on the beach?

opts.t: Phosphate is everywhere, but people only dig in two places.
opts.miss: Think about Why here. Did the rock form everywhere?

whyhere.credit: Map: Florida shapes from U.S. Census Bureau boundary files (public domain, via us-atlas). Springs: Florida’s first-magnitude springs. Phosphate mines: Bone Valley and Hamilton County mining areas (U.S. Geological Survey). Citrus: the leading citrus counties (USDA). Beaches: Florida’s sandy coast. Symbols are placed by hand and are approximate.
whyhere.win: Every pattern has a reason. The phosphate clusters are evidence of where the rock formed. That’s a clue.

photos.kicker: Look closer · a real Florida spring
photos.title: Where does spring water come from?
todo: Tap each number on the photo to read what it is.
Then match the clues to the labels below.

why.t: Manatee Springs, one of the blue dots on the springs layer, in north-central Florida.

photos.alt: A clear, blue-green spring pool surrounded by cypress trees, with a deep blue spot in the middle, swimmers on the left and cypress knees on the bank.
photos.credit: Manatee Springs, Manatee Springs State Park, Florida, Ebyabe, via Wikimedia Commons

hotspots.label: The deep blue spot
hotspots.t: This is the vent, the spring’s opening. Water from the underground limestone pours up out of it, every day of the year.

hotspots.label: Pale rock under the water
hotspots.t: Limestone. The water traveled through cracks and holes in rock like this before it came up here.

hotspots.label: Swimmers
hotspots.t: They show how big the spring is. The water stays about 72°F all year, even in winter.

hotspots.label: Cypress knees
hotspots.t: Bumps that grow up from the roots of cypress trees. Cypress trees grow where the ground stays wet.

task.q: Match each clue to a label on the photo.
task.win: You found it: spring water comes up from the limestone underground. That’s why springs cluster where that rock is close to the surface.

items.step: Where water comes up from underground
items.evid: Water pours up out of the spring’s vent.

items.step: The kind of rock the water flows through
items.evid: The water flows through limestone underground.

items.step: Shows how big the spring is
items.evid: Swimmers show the spring pool is big.

items.step: A tree that grows in wet ground
items.evid: Cypress trees grow around the wet spring.

pins.afterText: Marco put four pins on his map
pins.title: Test the pins
todo: Tap a numbered pin. The map zooms in.
Decide if Marco could find phosphate there, then pick the evidence.

why.t: A map is a record of real data. Checking an idea against data is how scientists test it.

pins.hint: Tap a numbered pin on the map.

pins.name: Near my cousin’s house in Miami
pins.note: My cousin has a big backyard!
pins.vmiss: Look closely. Are there any diamond symbols near Pin 1?
pins.q: What does the map show near Pin 1?

opts.t: No phosphate symbols anywhere near it, just the beach.
A cluster of phosphate mines.
opts.miss: Zoom in again. Is there a diamond near Miami?

opts.t: Orange groves all around it.
opts.miss: Look at the colors near Miami. Is it orange?

pins.why: No phosphate near Miami. The rock under Miami is limestone. People dig it for roads and cement, not fertilizer.

pins.name: The beach at Pensacola
pins.vmiss: Is there a diamond symbol anywhere near Pin 2?
pins.q: What does the map show at Pin 2?

opts.t: A beach on the coast, with no phosphate nearby.
The biggest phosphate cluster in Florida.
opts.miss: Zoom in again. Where is Pensacola compared to the diamonds?

opts.t: A cluster of springs.
opts.miss: Look at the symbols at Pin 2. Are they blue dots?

pins.why: Beach sand isn’t phosphate rock. The closest phosphate is hundreds of miles away.

pins.name: A cow pasture near Mulberry
pins.vmiss: Look right around Pin 3. What symbols do you see?
pins.q: What does the map show at Pin 3?

opts.t: It’s right inside the big cluster of phosphate mines.
Only beaches.
opts.miss: Is Mulberry on the coast? Look at the symbols around it.

opts.t: Only springs.
opts.miss: Look at the symbols around Pin 3. Are they blue dots or brown diamonds?

pins.why: Mulberry is in Bone Valley, Florida’s biggest phosphate area. That’s where the square lakes from Case 15 came from.

pins.name: The woods near White Springs
pins.vmiss: Look again. Is there a diamond symbol near Pin 4 too?
pins.q: What does the map show at Pin 4?

opts.t: A small cluster of phosphate mines right there.
Only springs, so no phosphate.
opts.miss: There are springs nearby, but look again. Are there diamonds too?

opts.t: Orange groves.
opts.miss: Look at the colors near Pin 4. Is it orange?

pins.why: Surprise! A second, smaller phosphate area is in north Florida, near White Springs. Phosphate is found in certain places, not everywhere.

pins.q: Which of Marco’s pins could have phosphate?

opts.t: All four pins.
opts.miss: Look at your test results. Did every pin pass?

opts.t: Pins 3 and 4, inside the phosphate clusters.
Only Pin 1.
opts.miss: What did the map show near Miami?

pins.win: You tested every pin with real map data. Two pins pass and two fail. That’s your last clue.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: The map key tells exactly what each symbol stands for.
Each symbol on a resource map marks a real place where something was found or measured.
The phosphate clusters on the map are where phosphate rock formed underground.
Springs on the map cluster where water-filled limestone is close to the surface.
We used the map to test Marco’s pins and ruled two of them out.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · dig here?
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes. Remember those square lakes? They were phosphate mines. Now Marco, one of our volunteers, wants to dig his own phosphate! He put four pins on a map, and he thinks phosphate is everywhere in Florida. Is he right? Let’s test his pins with a real resource map.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · guess first (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Before we look at any data, let’s guess. Pick a resource, then tap the blank map where you think it’s found. Do all four. Then press the button and see the real map. Don’t worry about being right. Scientists guess first so they can notice what surprises them.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. Point to a real map key, then sweep a hand along a coast for “pattern”.

part1.label: Part 1 · map layers (Clue 2)
part1.script: Busy maps can be confusing, so let’s turn on one layer at a time. Check a box in the map key, look at the symbols, and pick the pattern. Are they clustered together? Do they make a wide band? Or do they follow the coast? Watch the phosphate layer closely.

part3.label: Part 3 · why here? (Clue 3)
part3.script: Every pattern on a map has a reason. Look at each little map, then drag the reason that explains it. Is it the rock underground? The weather? The ocean? Be careful: one reason is a trick. After that, visit a real spring with me.

explore.label: Part 4 · test the pins (Clue 4)
explore.script: Time to test Marco’s idea. Tap a pin and the map zooms in. Could he find phosphate there? Decide, then pick what the map shows as your evidence. Test all four pins. You might find a surprise up north.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: which of Marco’s pins could have phosphate, and why only there? Then answer two questions, map one resource in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says maps are just pictures, and they don’t count as scientific evidence. Hmm. Think about how you tested Marco’s pins. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 16.01 (tradeoffs: benefits and costs of using resources).
closing.script: Case closed! Phosphate is only in a few places, and the map proved it. Sorry, Marco, no digging in the garden. Next time, a new week and a hard question: when we use a resource, how do we weigh what we gain against what we lose?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain why a resource is found in one place and not another?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: The map shows phosphate mines clustered in central Florida, where the rock formed.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “phosphate mines”, “clustered” and “central Florida”. Those words tell what, what pattern, and where. Small words like “the” and “in” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
